newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Libyan oil exploration looks to bright future.
newsitem.headline: Libyan oil exploration looks to bright future.

text.p: Libya's oil industry was set for a fruitful future as it reaped the benefits of rich and as yet untapped resources, Taleb M. Taleb, exploration manager of Libya's Sirte Oil Company, said on Wednesday.

Citing enhanced oil recovery techniques, Taleb said, "By directing exploration efforts along these lines, we feel that there is much more oil and gas to be discovered in Libya and we expect to see the Libyan petroleum business continuing to flourish well into the next century."

Speaking at the Africa Upstream 1996 conference, Taleb said that despite current economic sanctions and the withdrawal of U.S. oil companies from Libya, he believed the future of the country's oil industry was bright.
He emphasised that the "forced departure" of U.S. oil companies had had no adverse impact on Libya's oil production.

He said exploration to date had concentrated only on the relatively shallow, easily accessible basin targets and that deep trough and offshore fields held enormous unexplored potential which new technology made accessible.

"The deep troughs are virtually unexplored. Less than 150 wildcats (exploration drilling) have been drilled deeper than 13,000 feet and the presence of the Bu Attifel and Wadi fields prove that deep troughs are highly prospective," Taleb said.
Relating oil in place to depth, Taleb said that 68 percent of oil in place occured between 5,000 and 10,000 metres and 24 percent before 5,000 metres depth.
Taleb said that only a handful of wells had been drilled to explore for stratigraphic traps, four of which such units contained 80 percent of Libya's total oil in place.
He also said that offshore reserves were almost unexplored.
"Yet the Bouri discovery is the largest offshore field in North Africa and several other wells have tested significant amounts of oil and gas," he said.
From a basin point of view, the Bouri Field, together with three fields in the Murzak Basin, contain over 90 percent of all Libya's oil in place.

The application of enhanced oil recovery techniques had already proven that the recovery factor could be increased by 10-15 percent in some cases. Horizontal drilling was also yielding excellent results, Taleb said.
Libya is the second largest oil producer in Africa, after Nigeria. It has remaining proven reserves of 22.8 billion barrels and holds 35 percent of all African reserves.
Current oil production is 1.42 million barrels per day, limited by its OPEC quota, without which it could produce 1.7 million bpd, Taleb said.
